topics.title: Resistance and Ohm's law
topics.summary: Resistance is the voltage across a part divided by the current through it. For a wire it is set by the material, the length, and the cross-section (R = ρL/A); in an ohmic part such as a resistor it is the same at every voltage, so the current is proportional to the voltage.

prerequisiteNotes.charge_current: Current is charge per second and is the same at every point of a loop, so the current leaving a resistor equals the current entering it; resistance says how much current a part passes for each volt across it.
prerequisiteNotes.voltage_energy: Resistance is the voltage across a part divided by the current through it, so it needs the idea of a voltage between a part's two terminals; the energy each coulomb gives up crossing a resistor becomes heat.

lensNotes.physics: Inside a metal the field accelerates each free electron, which then scatters off the lattice's vibrations and impurities, in copper about every 2 × 10⁻¹⁴ s. The result is a net drift speed proportional to the field, so the current density is proportional to the field, J = E/ρ: Ohm's law at the scale of the material. For a uniform wire the field is V/L and the current is J·A, which gives R = ρL/A. Heating makes the lattice vibrate harder and scatter the electrons more often, so a metal's resistivity rises with temperature (copper about 0.39% per °C near 20 °C). In a diode the current is limited by a barrier at the junction instead, and grows exponentially with voltage. Pure copper is 1.68 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m with α ≈ 0.0040 per °C; wire tables use the annealed-copper standard for commercial wire, 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m and α = 0.00393 per °C at 20 °C, and so does this topic.
lensNotes.circuit: R = V/I gives a part's resistance at any operating point. A resistor is built so that R barely changes (a tolerance such as ±1%, and a temperature coefficient in ppm/°C). An ohmmeter passes its own small test current and reports V/I, so the circuit must be unpowered, and for a true reading the part must be out of circuit or have one leg lifted. Wires are resistors too: 10 m of 22 AWG copper is about 0.53 Ω.
lensNotes.math: For an ohmic part, I = V/R = G·V: on a plot of current against voltage it is a straight line through the origin with slope G = 1/R. A lamp or a diode gives a curve, and V/I differs from point to point. R = ρL/A is proportional to length and inversely proportional to area; area goes as the diameter squared, so doubling a wire's diameter quarters its resistance.

goals: Find a current, voltage, or resistance from the other two (V = IR), and a conductance from a resistance (G = 1/R)
Work out a copper wire's resistance from its length and cross-section (R = ρL/A), and the voltage a cable loses carrying a current
Tell ohmic parts from non-ohmic ones by their readings: a resistor's V/I stays constant, a lamp filament's rises as it heats, a diode's falls steeply
Measure resistance correctly: circuit unpowered, one leg lifted when other parts share the same two nodes
topics.intuition: Resistance is how many volts a part needs across it for each ampere through it; in a metal that ratio is fixed by the material, its temperature, and the conductor's shape, so twice the voltage gives twice the current.
topics.why: A voltage across a conductor sets up an electric field along it. The field accelerates the free electrons, but each one scatters off the vibrating atoms and impurities of the lattice about every 2 × 10⁻¹⁴ s and loses the velocity it gained. The result is a steady net drift proportional to the field, so the current is proportional to the voltage: that proportionality is Ohm's law, and the ratio V/I is the resistance. The energy the field gives the electrons between collisions passes to the lattice as heat, which is why a resistor gets warm. The material sets the resistivity ρ (how many free carriers it has and how often they scatter). A longer conductor needs more volts for the same field along it, and a wider one has more free electrons in each slice to carry the current, so R = ρL/A. Heating makes the lattice vibrate harder, so the electrons scatter more often: copper's resistance rises about 0.39% per °C, and a tungsten lamp filament's rises roughly tenfold between room temperature and its working temperature. A diode is different: current flows only as carriers get over a barrier at its junction, and the number that can do so grows exponentially with voltage, so no single resistance describes it.
topics.explanation:
Resistance is the voltage across a part divided by the current through it: R = V/I, in ohms (Ω). Rearranged, V = IR and I = V/R. Conductance is the inverse, G = 1/R = I/V, in siemens (S).

Ohm's law is the finding that for metals, and for resistors made to obey it, R is the same at every voltage, at a fixed temperature: double the voltage and the current doubles. Such parts are ohmic; their plot of current against voltage is a straight line through the origin with slope 1/R. Many parts are not ohmic. A lamp filament's resistance rises as it heats; a diode passes almost nothing until about 0.5 to 0.6 V, then its current climbs steeply. For them V/I changes from point to point.

For a uniform conductor, R = ρL/A: proportional to length, inversely proportional to cross-sectional area, with resistivity ρ set by the material (copper wire: 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m at 20 °C). Copper's resistance rises about 0.39% per °C.

The current leaving a resistor equals the current entering it; each coulomb gives up energy crossing it, measured as the voltage across it. Measure resistance with the circuit unpowered.

workedExample.problem: A 12 V pump draws 2.0 A through a two-conductor cable 8.0 m long; each conductor is 20 AWG copper, 0.518 mm² in cross-section. How much resistance does the cable add, and what voltage reaches the pump?
steps: The current goes out on one conductor and back on the other, so the copper in the loop is 2 × 8.0 m = 16 m long.
Area in square meters: 0.518 mm² = 0.518 × (10⁻³ m)² = 0.518 × 10⁻⁶ m².
Voltage lost in the cable: V = IR = 2.0 A × 0.531 Ω = 1.06 V, so the pump gets about 12 V − 1.06 V = 10.9 V.
The same 2.0 A flows in both conductors. The cable reduces the voltage, not the current: the field does 1.06 J of work on each coulomb crossing the copper, and that work becomes heat in the cable.

Size check: 20 AWG copper is about 33 mΩ per meter, and 16 m × 33 mΩ/m ≈ 0.53 Ω. An ohmmeter would struggle to show this: its own leads are often 0.1 to 0.3 Ω, so low resistances are measured with the leads zeroed out first, or with a separate pair of leads sensing the voltage.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. I (DC), ch. 2 "Ohm's Law", section "How voltage, current, and resistance relate"
sources.note: Ohm's finding: the current through a metal conductor is proportional to the voltage across it at a given temperature; E = IR, I = E/R, R = E/I.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. I (DC), ch. 2 "Ohm's Law", section "Nonlinear conduction"
sources.note: A resistor's current–voltage plot is a straight line; a lamp filament's resistance rises steeply as it heats, so its plot curves and V/I differs from point to point; R = E/I is better seen as a definition that holds for a class of materials.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. I (DC), ch. 12 "Physics of Conductors and Insulators", section "Specific resistance"
sources.note: R = ρl/A, with length in meters and area in square meters for ρ in Ω·m; a supply-and-return run counts both conductors in the voltage drop. Its table gives pure copper as 1.678 µΩ·cm; this topic uses the annealed-copper wire standard, 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. I (DC), ch. 12 "Physics of Conductors and Insulators", section "Temperature coefficient of resistance"
sources.note: Resistance changes by a factor α per °C from its 20 °C value; pure metals have positive coefficients, carbon and silicon negative. Its table gives pure copper as 0.004041 per °C; this topic uses 0.00393 per °C, the annealed-copper wire standard at 20 °C.

analogy.text: Slow, smooth (laminar) flow of a viscous liquid through a narrow channel follows a law of the same form as V = IR: the flow rate is proportional to the pressure difference across the channel, and the ratio, its flow resistance, is fixed by the liquid and the channel's shape. A longer channel resists more and a wider one less, and all the work the pressure does on the liquid becomes heat, as in a resistor.
analogy.breaksDown: A pipe's flow resistance falls with the fourth power of its radius, because the liquid is still at the walls and fastest in the middle, while a wire's falls only with its area (radius squared), because the current spreads evenly over the cross-section: twice the diameter gives a quarter of the resistance, not a sixteenth. Faster flow turns turbulent and stops being proportional, while a resistor stays ohmic across its whole rating. A hot liquid flows more easily, but a hot metal's resistance rises, because its electrons scatter more often off the harder-vibrating lattice.

templates.prompt: Find the current through R1. Assume an ideal battery.
templates.estimateHint: From the drawing, each value to one figure: I = V/R ≈ {V:fig1} V / ({R:fig1} Ω) ≈ {estI:fig1} A.
templates.explanation: Ohm's law: I = V/R = {V} / {R} = {answer}. A volt per ohm is an ampere, so volts divided by kilohms give milliamps directly.
hints: Resistance is volts per ampere. Rearrange it for the current.
I = V/R, with V in volts and R in ohms, gives amps.

misconceptions.feedback: You multiplied. A larger resistance passes less current for the same voltage, so the current is the voltage divided by the resistance: I = V/R.
That's upside down: ohms per volt. Resistance is volts per ampere, so amperes are volts divided by ohms: I = V/R.

followUps.prompt: An ammeter is inserted in the wire from R1 back to the battery's − terminal. What does it read?

choices.text: {I}, the same as the current into R1
choices.feedback: Right: charge can't pile up in R1 or vanish in it, so the current out equals the current in. What each coulomb gives up in R1 is energy, measured as the voltage across it.

choices.text: Less than {I}, because R1 used up part of the current
choices.feedback: A resistor doesn't use up current. Every coulomb that enters R1 leaves it; each one gives up {Wc} of energy crossing R1 ({V} is {Wc} per coulomb), and that energy heats R1.

choices.text: Almost zero, because R1 turns the current into heat
choices.feedback: R1 turns energy into heat, not current. If no current came out of R1, none could go in either: a resistor in a single loop sets the current for the whole loop.

choices.text: More than {I}, because the battery's − terminal attracts the electrons
choices.feedback: The current in a single loop is the same at every point, the terminals included. The − terminal has no extra pull that adds current on one side of R1.

followUps.explanation: In a single loop the current is the same at every point (charge and current). R1 sets how large that current is, I = V/R, and the energy each coulomb gives up crossing it, {Wc}, appears as heat in R1.

followUps.prompt: The battery is replaced with one of twice the voltage, {V2}. R1 stays within its ratings. What is R1's resistance now?

choices.text: Still {R}: a resistor is ohmic, so the current doubles along with the voltage and V/I stays the same
choices.feedback: Right: R1's resistance is set by its material and construction, not by the voltage across it. The current becomes 2 × {I}.

choices.text: Twice {R}, because R = V/I and V has doubled
choices.feedback: R = V/I with both V and I changing: twice the voltage gives twice the current through an ohmic part, so the ratio is unchanged.

choices.text: Half of {R}, because the higher voltage drives current through more easily
choices.feedback: A resistor's resistance is a property of its material and shape. The higher voltage gives a proportionally higher current; V/I stays {R}.

choices.text: You can't know it without measuring it again at the new voltage
choices.feedback: For a resistor you can: an ohmic part has the same V/I at every voltage within its ratings. That isn't true of a lamp or a diode, but R1 is a resistor.

followUps.explanation: Ohm's law says that for an ohmic part the current is proportional to the voltage, so V/I is a constant, the resistance. A resistor obeys it as long as it stays near its rated temperature; its datasheet gives the small drift as a temperature coefficient in ppm/°C.

templates.prompt: An unmarked resistor Rx is connected to a bench supply. A voltmeter across Rx reads {V} and an ammeter in series with it reads {I}. What is Rx?
templates.explanation: Resistance is the voltage across the part divided by the current through it: R = V/I = {V} / {I} = {answer}. Volts divided by milliamps give kilohms.
hints: Resistance is defined as a ratio of the two readings. Which one goes on top?
R = V/I: volts per ampere.

misconceptions.feedback: That's V × I, which is the power in watts (the next topic), not the resistance. Resistance is volts per ampere: R = V/I.
That's amperes per volt, the conductance G in siemens: the inverse of the resistance. Resistance is R = V/I.

templates.prompt: Circuit simulators solve for node voltages using conductances (amperes per volt) rather than resistances. What is the conductance of a {R} resistor? Answer in siemens (S); prefixes such as m and µ are fine.
templates.explanation: Conductance is the inverse of resistance: G = 1/R = 1 / {R} = {answer}. It is the current per volt: a conductance of {answer} passes that many amperes for each volt across the resistor (1 mS is 1 mA per volt). One over kilohms gives millisiemens.
hints: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance.
G = 1/R. One over kilohms gives millisiemens.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the resistance itself, in ohms. Conductance is its reciprocal, G = 1/R, in siemens.
That's 1 divided by the resistance in kilohms, which is the conductance in millisiemens, not siemens. Write it with the prefix (mS) or divide by 1000.

followUps.prompt: The {R} resistor sits across an ideal supply, which holds its voltage whatever is connected. A second {R} resistor is connected to the same two terminals, so it has the same voltage across it. What conductance does the supply see from the pair, and why?

choices.text: {G2}: each resistor alone conducts {G}, so it draws G·V, and the supply delivers both currents
choices.feedback: Right: each resistor has the full voltage across it, so each draws I = G·V as if it were alone. The supply's current is the sum, so the current per volt doubles: twice {G} = {G2}.

choices.text: {Gh}: two resistors put twice the resistance in the current's way, so half the current flows per volt
choices.feedback: That is true end to end (in series), where every coulomb must cross both resistors. Here each resistor is its own path between the same two terminals, and a second path can only add current.

choices.text: {G}, unchanged: the supply's voltage is the same, and the current divides between the two resistors, so each passes half what one did alone
choices.feedback: A resistor's current is set by the voltage across it, I = G·V, and each still has the full voltage, so each still passes {G} × V. The supply doesn't hand out a fixed total to be shared; it delivers whatever the resistors draw, now twice as much.

choices.text: {G4}: two resistors on the supply means double the current through each, and two of them, so four times the current per volt
choices.feedback: Each resistor's current depends only on its own voltage, I = G·V, and that voltage is the supply's, which hasn't changed. So each passes the same current as before; only the number of paths doubles, so the total is twice {G} = {G2}.

followUps.explanation: With both resistors on the same two terminals, each has the supply's voltage V across it and passes G·V. Charge is conserved where the wires join, so the supply delivers the sum: I = 2G·V, a conductance of {G2}, which is a resistance of {Rh}, half of {R}. Conductances of parts sharing the same two nodes simply add. This is why circuit simulators work in conductances: the currents of all the parts on a node add, so their conductances add straight into the equations, where resistances would need reciprocals every time.

templates.noDrawing: a unit conversion for one part; no circuit to analyze

templates.prompt: A spool holds {L} of {awg} AWG solid copper hookup wire, {Amm} mm² in cross-section. Copper wire has a resistivity of 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m at 20 °C. What is the resistance from one end of the wire to the other, at 20 °C?
templates.estimateHint: R = ρL/A with A in m²: {Amm} mm² ≈ {Am2:fig1} m² (1 mm² is 10⁻⁶ m²), and ρ ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m. So R ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m × {L:fig1} m / ({Am2:fig1} m²) ≈ {estR:fig1} Ω.
templates.explanation: R = ρL/A with the area in square meters: {Amm} mm² = {Amm} × 10⁻⁶ m². R = 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m × {L} / ({Amm} × 10⁻⁶ m²) = {answer}. Units: Ω·m × m / m² = Ω. That is small next to most circuit resistances, but not next to a low-resistance load or a heavy current (a cable feeding a 12 V load, for example).
hints: R = ρL/A. Every quantity must be in SI units first.
1 mm = 10⁻³ m, so 1 mm² = (10⁻³ m)² = 10⁻⁶ m².

misconceptions.feedback: The area is still in mm². Convert it first: 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m², so your answer is a million times too small.
You converted mm² with 10⁻³, the factor for millimeters. An area is a length squared: 1 mm² = (10⁻³ m)² = 10⁻⁶ m².
Length and area are swapped. A longer wire has more resistance (R ∝ L) and a thicker one less (R ∝ 1/A): R = ρL/A.

templates.noDrawing: about one length of wire on a spool; no circuit to analyze

templates.prompt: A 12 V battery feeds a work lamp through a two-conductor cable {L} long. Each conductor is {awg} AWG copper, {Amm} mm² in cross-section (ρ = 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m). The lamp draws {I} (measured in the cable). How much voltage is lost in the cable, both conductors together?
templates.explanation: Each conductor is R = ρL/A = 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m × {L} / ({Amm} × 10⁻⁶ m²) = {Rc}. The current goes out on one and back on the other, so the cable has 2 × {Rc} in series with the lamp. Voltage lost: V = I × 2R = {I} × 2 × {Rc} = {answer}, leaving about {Vlamp} for the lamp. This is why low-voltage loads far from their supply need thick cable: the volts lost depend only on the current and the cable's resistance, not on the supply, so on a 12 V system even 1 V lost is over 8% of the supply.
hints: Find the resistance of one conductor with R = ρL/A, area in m². How many conductors does the current pass through?
Out and back: the loop has 2 × {L} of copper. Then V = IR.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the drop in one conductor. The current returns through the second conductor too, and that drop adds: the loop has 2 × {L} of copper.
That's the voltage left for the lamp. The question asks for the voltage lost in the cable: I × (resistance of both conductors).

followUps.prompt: Compare the current in the conductor going to the lamp with the current in the conductor coming back from it.

choices.text: They are equal: the cable and lamp form one loop, and what the cable takes is energy, seen as voltage across each conductor
choices.feedback: Right: going once around the loop, the field does 12 J of work on each coulomb, a little in the outgoing conductor, most in the lamp, and a little in the return conductor, and every coulomb comes back.

choices.text: The return current is smaller, because the lamp and the outgoing conductor used some of it
choices.feedback: Neither the lamp nor the cable uses up charge. In a single loop the current is {I} at every point; what they take is energy, shown by the voltage across each of them.

choices.text: The return current is larger, because the lamp adds its own current to it
choices.feedback: A lamp is not a source; it can't add charge. One loop has one current, {I}, everywhere.

choices.text: The return current is zero, because the return conductor is at 0 V
choices.feedback: A conductor's voltage from ground says nothing about the current in it. The return conductor carries the full {I}; its voltage changes along its length by I times its resistance.

followUps.explanation: The voltage lost in each conductor is I × R for that conductor, with the same I in both. That is why the drop counts both conductors: the out and return paths are two resistances in the same loop.

templates.prompt: A 12 V relay's copper coil reads {Rc} on an ohmmeter at 20 °C. After the relay has been on for an hour, the supply is disconnected and the coil immediately reads {Rh}. Copper's resistance rises by α = 0.00393 of its 20 °C value per °C. What is the average temperature of the winding?
templates.explanation: R_T = R₂₀[1 + α(T − 20 °C)], so T = 20 °C + (R_T/R₂₀ − 1)/α. The resistance has risen by {Rh} − {Rc} = {dR}, which is {pct}% of {Rc}. Each °C adds 0.393%, so the rise is {pct} / 0.393 = {rise} above 20 °C, and the winding averages about {answer}. This resistance method is the standard way to find the temperature inside a winding, where no thermometer can reach: the winding's resistance measures the average copper temperature directly.
hints: Write R_hot = R_cold × [1 + α(T − 20 °C)] and solve for T.
First find R_hot/R_cold; the fraction above 1, divided by 0.00393, is the rise in °C.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the temperature rise above 20 °C. The question asks for the winding's temperature: add the 20 °C it started at.
α is a fraction of the 20 °C resistance per degree, not ohms per degree. Divide the change by {Rc} first: (R_hot/R_cold − 1)/α.

followUps.prompt: Why does the copper's resistance rise as it heats?

choices.text: The atoms of the lattice vibrate more, so the free electrons scatter more often and drift more slowly for the same field
choices.feedback: Right: in a metal the number of free electrons hardly changes with temperature; what changes is how often they scatter.

choices.text: The wire expands, so it gets longer and R = ρL/A rises
choices.feedback: Copper expands only about 0.0017% per °C, and its area grows too, which lowers R. The 0.39% per °C comes from the resistivity itself.

choices.text: Heat drives free electrons out of the copper, leaving fewer to carry the current
choices.feedback: A metal keeps its free electrons; their number barely changes with temperature. (In a semiconductor, heating frees more carriers, which is why its resistance falls.)

choices.text: The coil's current heats the copper's electrons, and hot electrons carry less current
choices.feedback: The free electrons in a metal move at about 10⁶ m/s at any temperature; a few tens of degrees barely change that. The rise comes from more frequent scattering off the warmer lattice.

followUps.explanation: Resistivity comes from the free electrons scattering off the lattice's vibrations and impurities. Warmer atoms vibrate with larger amplitude, so collisions come more often and the drift for a given field is smaller. For copper near room temperature that adds about 0.39% of the 20 °C resistance per °C.

templates.noDrawing: about a coil's resistance measured on its own with an ohmmeter

templates.prompt: A 12 V incandescent lamp is lit from a {V} battery and draws {I}. What is the filament's resistance while it is lit?
templates.explanation: The resistance at this operating point is R = V/I = {V} / {I} = {answer}. That is the hot filament's resistance; a lamp's V/I is only meaningful at the point where it was measured, because the filament's resistance depends on its temperature.
hints: Resistance is the voltage across a part divided by the current through it.
R = V/I with the lamp running.

misconceptions.feedback: That's V × I, the power in watts (the next topic). The resistance is the voltage divided by the current: R = V/I.
That's amperes per volt, the conductance. The resistance is volts per ampere: R = V/I.

followUps.prompt: With the lamp out of the circuit and at room temperature, an ohmmeter across it reads about {Rcold}. Why is that so different?

choices.text: Tungsten's resistance rises steeply with temperature; lit, the filament is at over 2000 °C and its resistance is more than ten times its cold value
choices.feedback: Right: the filament's lattice vibrates far harder at white heat, so the electrons scatter much more often. The lamp is not ohmic over its working range.

choices.text: The ohmmeter is inaccurate at low resistances and reads far too low
choices.feedback: A meter's lead resistance makes low readings too high by a few tenths of an ohm, not ten times too low. The filament really is more than ten times lower in resistance when cold.

choices.text: The lamp is faulty: a good lamp reads the same resistance cold and lit
choices.feedback: Every tungsten filament lamp shows this. Its resistance follows its temperature, and the temperature changes by over 2000 °C between cold and lit.

choices.text: Resistance depends on voltage: the meter's small test voltage always gives a small resistance
choices.feedback: A resistor reads the same on an ohmmeter as V/I gives at full voltage. The filament's resistance changes with its temperature, which the voltage only sets indirectly through the heating.

followUps.explanation: Cold, the filament's resistance is less than a tenth of its hot value, so at switch-on the current briefly jumps to more than ten times the running current until the filament heats, within tens of milliseconds. This inrush is why filament lamps usually fail at switch-on, and why a lamp's V/I depends on where it is measured.

templates.prompt: Resistor R1 = {R} sits across a {V} supply. The supply is turned up to {new_V}. What happens to the current through R1?

feedback.same: A resistor doesn't hold its current at one value. Its resistance stays {R}, and the current is whatever the voltage across it can drive through that resistance, I = V/R: a larger voltage sets up a stronger field along the resistor, which drives the charge through it faster.
feedback.down: A resistor doesn't resist more at a higher voltage; its resistance stays {R}. A larger voltage across the same resistance sets up a stronger field along it, which drives the charge through it faster: I = V/R.

templates.explanation: The resistor is ohmic: its resistance stays {R} whatever the voltage. I = V/R goes from {V}/{R} = {before} to {new_V}/{R} = {after}, exactly twice. (A lamp would not double, because its filament heats up and its resistance rises.)
hints: Does the resistor's resistance depend on the voltage across it?
I = V/R with R fixed: what does doubling V do?

templates.prompt: A {L} run of copper wire with a {Amm} mm² cross-section is replaced by a run of the same wire {new_L} long. What happens to the resistance of the run?

feedback.same: The material and thickness are the same, but there is twice as much wire for the current to pass through, and each meter is a resistance in series with the next.
feedback.down: Adding wire can't make it easier to push the current through: each meter is a resistance in series with the next, and for the same current each meter needs the same voltage across it.

templates.explanation: R = ρL/A with the same ρ and A: R is proportional to length, {before} → {after}. Seen another way: for a given current, each meter of wire needs the same field and so the same voltage, and the voltages of the meters add.
hints: Think of the run as many one-meter pieces, one after another.
R = ρL/A: only L changes.
templates.noDrawing: about one wire's dimensions; no circuit to analyze

templates.prompt: A {L} run of round copper wire {d} mm in diameter is replaced by copper wire {new_d} mm in diameter, the same length. What happens to its resistance?

feedback.up: A thicker wire doesn't oppose the current more: each slice of it holds more free electrons to share the same current, so each electron drifts more slowly and the wire needs a weaker field along it.
feedback.same: The length and material are the same, but resistance also depends on the cross-section, R = ρL/A. A larger area puts more free electrons in each slice to share the same current, so each drifts more slowly, and the field (and so the voltage) needed to drive that current is not the same as before.

whatIf.factorHint: R = ρL/A, and the area A = πd²/4 depends on the diameter squared. Work out what doubling d does to A first, then what that does to R. (A fourth-power law belongs to liquid flow in a pipe, not to current in a wire.)

templates.explanation: R = ρL/A, and the cross-section of a round wire is A = πd²/4. Twice the diameter gives four times the area, so a quarter of the resistance: {before} → {after}. That square law is why wire gauges step quickly: every 3 AWG sizes roughly double the area and halve the resistance per meter.
hints: R depends on the area, not directly on the diameter. How does a circle's area change when its diameter doubles?
A = πd²/4: doubling d multiplies A by 4.
templates.noDrawing: about one wire's dimensions; no circuit to analyze

templates.prompt: A relay coil wound from copper reads {Rc} at {T} and runs from a fixed 12 V supply. After a long time switched on, the winding warms to {new_T}. Copper's resistance rises by 0.00393 of its 20 °C value per °C. What happens to the coil current?

feedback.up: Heat doesn't help the free electrons through the metal: the lattice vibrates harder and scatters them more often, so the coil's resistance rises, and at a fixed 12 V the current is I = V/R.
feedback.same: The supply voltage is fixed, but the coil's resistance is not: copper's resistance rises about 0.39% per °C. With the same 12 V across a different resistance, I = V/R changes.

templates.explanation: At 20 °C, I = 12 V / {Rc} = {before}. At 70 °C the resistance is {Rc} × (1 + 0.00393 × 50) = 1.197 × {Rc}, so I = {after}, about 16% less. A relay's magnetic pull depends on the coil current, so a hot coil pulls in less firmly; relay datasheets state the must-operate voltage at a given temperature (usually 23 °C ambient), and some give a higher hot-start value, because a hot coil needs more voltage to reach the same current.
hints: What does heating do to copper's resistance?
templates.noDrawing: about a coil on a fixed supply; the change is in the coil's material, not the circuit

templates.prompt: A 12 V filament lamp and a wirewound power resistor each draw {I6} when connected, one at a time, across a 6 V supply. Each is then connected across 12 V. Which statement about the currents at 12 V is right?

choices.text: The resistor draws {I12}; the lamp draws more than {I6} but less than {I12}
choices.feedback: Right: the resistor's V/I stays fixed, so its current doubles. The lamp's filament runs hotter at 12 V, its resistance rises, and its current grows less than in proportion.

choices.text: Both draw {I12}: by Ohm's law, twice the voltage gives twice the current
choices.feedback: That holds only for an ohmic part. The filament gets hotter at 12 V, and hot tungsten has a higher resistance, so the lamp's current less than doubles.

choices.text: The resistor draws {I12}; the lamp draws more than {I12}, because a hotter filament conducts better
choices.feedback: Metals conduct worse when hot: the hotter lattice scatters the free electrons more often. The filament's resistance rises, so its current less than doubles.

choices.text: Both still draw {I6}: each part limits the current to its own value
choices.feedback: Neither part fixes its current. A resistor fixes the ratio V/I, so its current doubles; the lamp's current rises too, though by less.

templates.explanation: Ohm's law is a property of a material at a fixed temperature, not a law every part obeys. At 6 V both parts have V/I = 6 V / {I6}. At 12 V the resistor still has that ratio and draws {I12}. The lamp's filament heats further, its resistance rises, and its current lands somewhere between {I6} and {I12}: its I–V plot bends over instead of running straight.
hints: Which of the two parts changes temperature a great deal when the voltage doubles?
A metal's resistance rises with temperature. What does that do to the lamp's current at 12 V?
templates.noDrawing: compares two parts' I–V behavior; no particular circuit

templates.prompt: A small silicon diode is measured on a bench in its forward direction. Typical readings: 0.30 V gives 2 µA, 0.60 V gives 0.8 mA, and 0.70 V gives 6 mA. What do the readings say about the diode and Ohm's law?

choices.text: V/I falls from about 150 kΩ to about 120 Ω over these readings: the diode has no single resistance, so it is not ohmic
choices.feedback: Right: an ohmic part keeps one V/I at every voltage. The diode's current grows exponentially with voltage, so its V/I changes by more than a factor of a thousand.

choices.text: The diode is ohmic: V = IR holds at every reading, with R worked out from that reading
choices.feedback: V/I can be worked out at any point for any part; that just defines R there. Ohm's law says more: that the ratio is the same at every voltage. Here it changes over a thousandfold, so the diode is not ohmic.

choices.text: Its resistance is about 120 Ω; the low-voltage readings are meter errors
choices.feedback: The readings are what silicon junctions really do: almost no current until about 0.5 to 0.6 V, then a steep rise. A meter error wouldn't give a smooth exponential pattern.

choices.text: Every part's resistance falls as the voltage rises; a resistor would show the same pattern
choices.feedback: A resistor keeps the same V/I at every voltage, and a metal filament's V/I rises as it heats. The steep fall is particular to the diode's junction.

templates.explanation: For each reading R = V/I: 0.30 V / 2 µA = 150 kΩ, 0.60 V / 0.8 mA = 750 Ω, 0.70 V / 6 mA ≈ 117 Ω. In a diode the current is set by how many carriers get over the barrier at the junction, and that number grows exponentially with voltage. Its I–V plot is a sharp curve, not a straight line, so Ohm's law does not describe it; diode models do (the Diodes unit).
hints: Work out V/I for each reading. Is it the same each time?
Ohmic means one value of V/I at every voltage.
templates.noDrawing: about one part's I–V readings; no circuit to analyze

templates.prompt: Two resistors, A and B, are swept from 0 to 5 V on a curve tracer, which plots current (vertical) against voltage (horizontal). Both give straight lines through the origin. At 5 V, A passes {IA} and B passes {IB}, so A's line is the steeper. Which has the larger resistance?

choices.text: B: the slope of a current–voltage line is I/V = 1/R, so the shallower line is the larger resistance
choices.feedback: Right: B needs more volts for each ampere. Its resistance is 5 V / {IB} = {RB}, against {RA} for A.

choices.text: A: the steeper line rises faster, which means more resistance
choices.feedback: With current on the vertical axis the slope is amperes per volt, the conductance. A steep line passes a lot of current per volt: a small resistance.

choices.text: Neither: both lines are straight, so both have the same resistance
choices.feedback: Straight lines through the origin mean both are ohmic, each with a constant V/I. Their slopes differ, so their resistances differ.

choices.text: You can't tell without knowing each resistor's power rating
choices.feedback: The power rating says how much heat a resistor can take, not its resistance. The plot alone gives each one's V/I.

templates.explanation: On an I–V plot the slope is ΔI/ΔV = 1/R. A is {RA} and B is {RB}: A's line through (5 V, {IA}) is the steeper one, and B's line through (5 V, {IB}) is shallower. Plots with voltage on the vertical axis exist too, so always check the axes before reading resistance from a slope.
hints: What are the units of the slope when current is vertical and voltage horizontal?
Slope = ΔI/ΔV = 1/R.
templates.noDrawing: about reading an I–V plot; no circuit to analyze

templates.prompt: On an unpowered board, R1 is marked {R1} (±5%). A meter on its ohms range across R1's two pins, nodes x and y, reads {Rread}. Which step tells you whether R1 itself is good?

choices.text: Unsolder one of R1's legs and measure it again, so the meter's test current can only flow through R1
choices.feedback: Right: with one leg lifted, R1 is the only path between the meter's probes, so V/I is R1's resistance.

choices.text: Nothing more: the meter reads R1, so R1 has drifted to {Rread} and must be replaced
choices.feedback: The meter reads everything connected between x and y. Its test current also flows through R2 and R3, so it sees more current for its test voltage and reports a lower V/I than R1 alone.

choices.text: Power the board and measure again, so the parts are in their working state
choices.feedback: An ohmmeter works out R from its own test current and the voltage it measures. With the board powered, the circuit's own voltages and currents add to those, so the reading is meaningless, and the meter can be damaged.

choices.text: Switch to a higher ohms range, which keeps R2 and R3 out of the reading
choices.feedback: The range sets the meter's test current and resolution, not where that current flows. R2 and R3 still connect x to y on every range.

templates.explanation: An ohmmeter drives a small test current between its probes and reports V/I. In circuit, R2 and R3 form a second path from x to y, so part of the test current goes that way and the reading, {Rread}, is lower than R1's {R1}. Lifting one leg of R1 removes the other path. An in-circuit reading can only ever be equal to or lower than the part's own value when only resistors are involved, so a reading above the marked value does point at the part. Here {Rread} is exactly 10 kΩ ∥ (R2 + R3), what a healthy R1 would give, but that check trusts R2 and R3; lifting a leg doesn't.
hints: What, besides R1, connects node x to node y?
The meter reports its test voltage divided by the total current it sends between its probes.

followUps.prompt: Why does the second path make the reading lower than R1, never higher?

choices.text: R1 and the R2–R3 path join the same two nodes, so whatever voltage appears across x–y drives current through both; the meter's V/I is that voltage over the sum of the two currents, which is less than R1
choices.feedback: Right: each path adds current. The meter can't tell which path the current took; it divides its voltage by the total.

choices.text: R2 and R3 are in series with R1 and take part of the test voltage, leaving less across R1
choices.feedback: R2–R3 is not in series with R1: it connects x to y by itself, so whatever voltage is across R1 is across R2–R3 too. It is a second current path.

choices.text: The test current splits, so less flows through R1 and it seems smaller
choices.feedback: If the meter divided its voltage by R1's share of the current alone, it would read exactly R1. It divides by the total current between its probes, and the second path adds to that total, so the reading falls below R1.

choices.text: R2 and R3 cancel part of R1's resistance
choices.feedback: Resistances don't cancel. A second path between the same two nodes simply passes extra current for the same voltage.

followUps.explanation: The meter measures the whole network between its probes: V_test / (I_R1 + I_R2R3). Every extra path between x and y adds current, so an in-circuit resistance reading is never above the part's own value (with only resistors around it).

templates.prompt: A {V} supply feeds a heater element (a {R1} power resistor) through a lead and connector of about 0.1 Ω. When the circuit is healthy, the meters read {h0} at the supply terminals, {h1} across the heater, and {h2} through it. The heater is not heating properly. Using Ohm's law on each part, which fault explains the readings below?

probes.label: Voltage at the supply terminals (black lead on ground)
Voltage across the heater (black lead on ground)

faults.text: The connector is corroded and has built up about 2 Ω
faults.feedback: A corroded connector would leave the supply at full voltage but lose part of it before the heater: the heater would see a lower voltage, with a current that still gives V/I = {R1}.
faults.why: The supply holds its voltage, but only part of it reaches the heater; the rest is across the connector, I × R_connector. The heater's own V/I is still {R1}, so the heater is fine.

faults.text: The heater element has degraded to ten times its rated resistance
faults.feedback: A degraded element would still get nearly the full supply voltage, but its V/I would be far above {R1}, so the current would be much smaller.
faults.why: Nearly the full voltage is across the heater, yet the current is a tenth of normal: V/I across the heater is ten times {R1}. The fault is in the element.

faults.text: The heater element is open (burned through)
faults.feedback: An open element would pass no current at all; with nothing flowing, no voltage is lost in the lead, so the full supply voltage would appear across the open element's terminals.
faults.why: Zero current, and the full supply voltage across the heater's terminals: no current means no drop in the lead (V = IR = 0), so the break must be in the element itself.

faults.text: The supply has been set to half its voltage by mistake
faults.feedback: A supply at half voltage would show half voltage at its own terminals, with nearly all of it across the heater.
faults.why: The supply terminals read half the normal voltage, and nearly all of it reaches the heater. The heater's V/I is still {R1}; it just has half the voltage across it.

faults.feedback: A broken lead would stop the current, and the heater, now cut off from the supply, would read 0 V across it while the supply terminals still read full voltage.
faults.why: The supply reads full voltage, but the heater has 0 V across it and no current: the break is between them, in the lead.

templates.explanation: Apply R = V/I to each piece. Across the heater, V/I equal to {R1} means the element is fine; far above {R1} means the element has changed. The difference between the supply and heater readings is the voltage across the lead and connector, I × R_lead: 0.1 Ω × {h2}, at most a few tenths of a volt when healthy, and much more if a connection has gone bad. Zero current with full voltage across the heater means a break in the element; zero current with zero across it means the break is in the lead.
hints: Work out V/I across the heater from its two readings. Is it still {R1}?
Then compare the supply voltage with the heater voltage: the difference is across the lead and connector.

templates.prompt: The valve no longer opens reliably. Which fault explains these readings?

fault.netlist:
battery, cable and valve
V1 a 0 12
RW1 a b 0.2
RL1 b c {RL:spice}
RW2 c 0 0.2

faults.text: The connection at the battery's + terminal is corroded and has built up about 8 Ω
faults.feedback: A corroded + connection would sit in series ahead of the valve. The current would fall, the volts lost across the corroded joint would leave the valve's + terminal well below 12 V, and its − terminal would still read only a fraction of a volt.
faults.why: The valve's + terminal has lost several volts, yet its − terminal still reads only I × 0.2 Ω. The missing volts are across something between the battery's + terminal and the valve, with a resistance far above a good conductor's 0.2 Ω.

faults.text: The connection at the battery's − terminal is corroded and has built up about 8 Ω
faults.feedback: A corroded − terminal connection would sit in the return path: the valve's + terminal would stay near 12 V, but its − terminal would sit several volts above the battery's − terminal, because the current would drop I × 8 Ω in that connection.
faults.why: The valve's − terminal should be within a fraction of a volt of the battery's − terminal, and it reads several volts. By V = IR, volts appear where the resistance is, so the return path, between the valve and the battery's − terminal, has a resistance far above 0.2 Ω: the corroded connection at that terminal.

faults.text: The valve's coil is open (a broken winding)
faults.feedback: An open coil would stop the current. With no current, neither conductor would drop anything, so the + terminal would read the full 12 V and the − terminal 0 V: the whole 12 V would be across the break inside the coil.
faults.why: The + terminal reads the full 12 V and the − terminal 0 V. No current flows, so neither conductor drops anything (V = I × 0.2 Ω = 0), and all 12 V is across the valve. A good coil with 12 V across it would conduct, so the break is inside the coil.

faults.feedback: A broken return would stop the current. With no current through the coil, the coil would drop nothing, so both valve terminals would read the full 12 V, and the 12 V would be across the break in the return.
faults.why: Both valve terminals read 12 V. No current flows, so the coil drops nothing and its − terminal sits at the same potential as its + terminal. The full 12 V is across the gap, and the gap is in the return conductor.

faults.feedback: A broken + conductor would cut the valve off from the battery's + terminal. Both valve terminals would read 0 V, because the coil and the return still connect them to the battery's − terminal.
faults.why: Both valve terminals read 0 V. They still connect to the battery's − terminal through the coil and the return conductor, but nothing connects them to the + terminal, so the break is in the + conductor.

templates.explanation: Apply V = IR to each piece of the loop. When healthy, the current is 12 V / ({RL} + 0.4 Ω) = {I}, so each good conductor drops only {I} × 0.2 Ω = {Vc}: the + terminal reads about {h0} and the − terminal about {h1}. Several volts across a piece of wire mean resistance where there should be almost none: the volts appear where the resistance is. When the loop is broken, no current flows, so every intact piece drops nothing (V = IR = 0) and the full 12 V is across the break; finding where the 12 V sits finds the break. This is voltage-drop testing: it finds a bad connection with the circuit working and carrying its real current, which an ohmmeter on the disconnected circuit can miss.
hints: In a healthy circuit, how many volts should a 0.2 Ω conductor drop at this current?
With no current, an intact part drops nothing (V = IR = 0), so the full 12 V is across the break.

followUps.prompt: The return conductor breaks. Why does the valve's − terminal then read the full 12 V, not 0 V?

choices.text: No current flows, so the coil drops nothing (V = IR = 0): its − terminal sits at the potential of its + terminal, and the 12 V is across the break
choices.feedback: Right: a resistance carrying no current has no voltage across it, so the coil simply passes the + terminal's potential through to its − terminal.

choices.text: Charge piles up at the break and raises the voltage of everything on the valve's side
choices.feedback: The reading needs no pile of charge to explain it. With no current the coil drops nothing (V = IR = 0), so its − end is at the same potential as its + end, which is wired to the battery's + terminal.

choices.text: The coil stores 12 V like a capacitor and holds it after the circuit breaks
choices.feedback: The reading doesn't fade with time; it stays as long as the break does. It is set by Ohm's law: the coil carries no current, so it has no voltage across it, and its − end sits at the + terminal's potential.

choices.text: The break lifts the battery's − terminal to 12 V
choices.feedback: The battery still holds 12 V between its terminals, and the meter's black lead is on its − terminal. What changed is that no current flows through the coil, so the coil no longer drops anything.

followUps.explanation: A voltage across a resistance needs a current through it: V = IR. With the loop broken anywhere, every intact part carries zero current and drops zero volts, so the potential of each battery terminal reaches right up to its side of the break. The whole 12 V is therefore across the break itself, which is why a voltmeter across an open switch or a burned-through fuse reads the full supply.

battery, cable and valve
V1 a 0 12
RW1 a b 0.2
RL1 b c {RL:spice}
RW2 c 0 0.2
schematic.noBuild: the two 0.2 Ω resistors are models of the cable's conductors, not parts

templates.prompt: Choose the largest E24 value for the sense resistor R1 that keeps the voltage across it at or below 100 mV at full load.

design.resultLabel: Voltage across R1 at full load

templates.explanation: The full-load current, {I}, flows through R1, so the voltage across it is V = I·R. At most 100 mV means R ≤ 100 mV / {I} = {Rmax}. Take the E24 value at or just below that and check I × R: the next E24 value up would put more than 100 mV across R1. Within that limit, larger is better: a bigger signal stands further above the reading circuit's offset and noise. R1 also takes at most 100 mV × {I} = {Pmax} of heat, so choose its power rating above that. The circuit that reads R1 amplifies its small voltage; every millivolt across R1 is taken from the motor's 12 V and turned into heat, which is why a sense resistor is kept to a small fraction of the supply. At start-up a motor draws several times its full-load current for a moment (standing still, only its winding resistance limits the current), so R1 must survive that surge, and the circuit reading it sees several times 100 mV.
hints: The voltage across R1 is the motor current times R1. Which R would give exactly 100 mV? The E24 values per decade: 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.5, 1.6, 1.8, 2.0, 2.2, 2.4, 2.7, 3.0, 3.3, 3.6, 3.9, 4.3, 4.7, 5.1, 5.6, 6.2, 6.8, 7.5, 8.2, 9.1.
R ≤ 100 mV / {I}; then take the E24 value at or just below it.

followUps.prompt: Why not use 1 Ω for R1 and get a much larger signal?

choices.text: With {I} through it, 1 Ω would drop {V1o} of the motor's 12 V and turn {P1o} into heat
choices.feedback: Right: R1 carries the whole motor current, so V = I·R comes out of the motor's supply. With 1 Ω the motor would run slower on less voltage, and R1 would need a large rating to carry the heat.

choices.text: It would raise the motor current above {I}, since R1 adds to the load
choices.feedback: R1 sits in the motor's only path, so it adds resistance to that path; it can't raise the current. A part across the supply adds a second path and more current; a part in the path takes voltage.

choices.text: Nothing stops it: R1 carries the same {I} whatever its value, so the motor is unaffected
choices.feedback: The current is the same through R1 and the motor, but the 12 V is shared: whatever R1 drops, I·R, the motor no longer gets. With 1 Ω that is about {V1o}, far more than a 100 mV budget.

choices.text: A resistor of 1 Ω or more can't carry {I}
choices.feedback: A resistor's value doesn't limit the current it can carry; the heat does. 1 Ω at {I} turns about {P1o} into heat, so it would need a part rated for that, but it could carry the current.

followUps.explanation: A sense resistor sits in the current's only path, so everything across it is lost to the load and turned into heat. Designers choose the smallest voltage the reading circuit can measure accurately, often 50 to 100 mV at full scale, and amplify it.

templates.prompt: Expected {Ve} at out, but a meter from out to ground reads {Vm}. R1 measures its marked value with one lead lifted. Find the actual value of R2.
templates.explanation: R1 is good, so it gives the current: it has 12 V − {Vm} = {VR1} across it, so I = {VR1} / {R1} = {I}. The same current flows through R2 (one path; charge doesn't pile up between them), with {Vm} across it: R2 = {Vm} / {I} = {answer}. It should be {R2}: exactly a factor of ten off, the mark of a wrong part being installed (a chip resistor from the wrong reel, or a banded one with its multiplier misread: red, orange and brown look alike), not of a resistor that drifted.
hints: R1 is good. What do R1's value and the voltage across it tell you?
I = (12 V − V_out)/R1, and the same current flows through R2: R2 = V_out / I.

misconceptions.feedback: You took the current as 12 V / R1, as if R1 had the whole supply across it. R1 has only 12 V − {Vm} = {VR1} across it, so I = {VR1} / {R1} = {I}.
The reading isn't proportional to R2: a different R2 also changes the current through both resistors. Find the current from R1 first, then R2 = V_out / I.
That ratio is upside down: it is R1 × V_R1 / V_out. R2 has V_out across it, so R2 = R1 × V_out / V_R1.
That is R2's intended value, which would put {Ve} at out. The meter reads {Vm}: find the current from R1, then R2 = V_out / I.

followUps.prompt: Could you find R2 from the reading at out alone, without R1's value?

choices.text: No: the reading fixes only the ratio of R2 to R1, so R1's value is needed to turn it into ohms
choices.feedback: Right: {Vm} at out says R2 has {Vm} of the 12 V and R1 the other {VR1}, so R2/R1 = {Vm} / {VR1}. Any pair with that ratio reads the same; R1 sets the scale.

choices.text: Yes: R2 = V_out / I, with the current I = 12 V / R2
choices.feedback: That uses R2 to find R2. The current is set by both resistors, I = 12 V / (R1 + R2), so without R1 there are two unknowns and one reading.

choices.text: Yes: a resistor's value follows from the voltage across it alone
choices.feedback: The voltage across a resistor is I·R: the same voltage fits a large R with a small current or a small R with a large one. You need the current, and R1 provides it.

choices.text: No: you would also need the current the meter draws
choices.feedback: A multimeter on its volts range has about 10 MΩ across its leads, so it draws {Vm} / 10 MΩ = {Im}, far too little to matter against these resistors. What's missing without R1 is the current through R2.

followUps.explanation: A voltage reading at the joint of two resistors fixes their ratio, not their values. One known resistance turns the ratio into ohms. To confirm, lift one lead of R2 and measure it.
